title: Chest pain on day 5 after hip fracture surgery
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 47-year-old builder with sudden pleuritic chest pain on day 5 after fixation of a right neck of femur fracture, choosing his investigations, then interpreting his observations, ECG, bloods and CT pulmonary angiogram, managing a haemodynamically stable pulmonary embolism with the orthopaedic team, and safety-netting.
focus: Post-operative pleuritic chest pain: recognising, investigating and managing pulmonary embolism
stem: You are the surgical resident covering the orthopaedic ward of a busy metropolitan hospital. Chong Loh, a 47-year-old builder, is 5 days after an operation to fix a right neck of femur fracture. His nurse has asked you to review him because he is complaining of chest pain.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Loh, perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining, and tell the examiner which investigations you would request (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you his observations, ECG, blood results and CT pulmonary angiogram report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Chong Loh, a 47-year-old builder. You are 5 days after an operation to fix a broken right hip (neck of femur). You are sitting in bed, a little short of breath, frightened and holding your chest. Stay the same throughout Part 1: the pain stays at 5/10 and you can speak in full sentences. You settle a little if the candidate explains what they are doing and reassures you calmly; you become more anxious if they ignore your fear. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Nurse's report (the examiner gives this at the start, and the observations when asked): "This is Chong in bed 12. He's day 5 after a right neck of femur fixation and he's just told me he has chest pain. His obs at 08:00 were all normal. I've just done another set." Now (14:20): heart rate 124 regular, blood pressure 132/84, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 93% on room air, temperature 37.6 °C, alert, pain 5/10. The nurse can do an ECG, insert a cannula and take bloods if asked.

Opening line: "Doctor, I have chest pain!"

The chest pain (give only when asked):

  • Where: point to the centre and right lower side of your chest. It does not spread anywhere.
  • When: "It came on quite quickly around 30 minutes ago."
  • What it feels like: "It feels like a sharp pain." 5 out of 10.
  • Worse: taking a deep breath. Not better: with the Panadol the nurse gave you or with changing position. Sitting forward does not help.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Breathlessness: yes, for about 2 hours, before the pain started. "I just can't get a full breath."
  • Right leg: your right calf has been sore, swollen and red since last night (about 12 hours). You thought it was from the operation.
  • No: cough, coughing up blood, fainting or feeling faint, palpitations, fever, sweats, nausea or vomiting.
  • No: crushing or tight pain, pain into the arm, neck or jaw, tearing pain going through to your back, waking up breathless at night, needing more pillows, swelling of the left leg.
  • No: burning pain, reflux, pain linked to food, trouble swallowing, upper tummy pain.
  • No: injury to your chest in the fall, a tender spot on your ribs, or any history of anxiety or panic attacks.
  • General: no night sweats or weight loss. Tired from being in hospital.

This admission (only if asked): you fell from a height at work (a scaffold, about 2 metres) and landed on your right hip. No other significant injuries. The operation went fine with no complications that you were told about. The physio got you up with a frame on the first two days, but it hurts, so you have mostly stayed in bed and only get up to the toilet. The wound has not bled and the dressing is dry. No black stools or blood in the urine.

Past history: appendix out at age 14. Nothing else. No previous blood clots, no cancer, no bleeding problems. If specifically asked about your weight: "I'm a big bloke. The nurse said my BMI is about 31."

Medicines: "I've been having regular Panadol, and ibuprofen only when I need it for the pain. I've also been getting the injection in the tummy to thin the blood. I think they called it Clexane." You have had it every evening, including last night. No regular medicines before this admission.

Allergies: none, including no reaction to X-ray dye.

Family history: both parents alive, both have high blood pressure. Your father had an operation for bowel cancer this year and is recovering well. Your son (17) is healthy. No one in the family has had blood clots.

Social history: you smoke 20 cigarettes a day and have since age 20. You haven't been able to smoke in hospital and miss it. Alcohol is minimal: occasionally 1 or 2 beers at social events. You live in a suburban house with your wife and son. Your diet is a lot of fatty food and takeaway. Building work is physically demanding; no exercise outside work.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: "No idea why my chest would be hurting." Concern: "I'm worried if this is a heart attack!" You want to know what is going on and to be fixed.

Exam findings (examiner gives these when the candidate says what they examine)

  • Observations: as the nurse's set above. 08:00 set: HR 84, BP 130/82, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, T 36.8 °C.
  • General: anxious, mildly breathless, speaking in full sentences, not sweaty, not cyanosed. Large build (98 kg, BMI 31).
  • Cardiovascular: pulse 124, regular. BP right arm 132/84, left arm 128/82. JVP not raised. Heart sounds dual, no murmur, no loud P2, no rub. No right ventricular heave. Peripheries warm, capillary refill 2 seconds.
  • Respiratory: trachea central, expansion equal, percussion resonant except slight dullness at the right base, slightly reduced air entry at the right base, no crackles, wheeze or pleural rub.
  • Chest wall: no tenderness, bruising or deformity; pressing does not reproduce the pain.
  • Legs: right calf visibly swollen, circumference 41 cm (left 37 cm) measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity; warm, red, tender along the deep veins of the calf; pitting oedema to mid-shin. Left leg normal.
  • Right hip wound: clean and dry, staples intact, no ooze, haematoma or redness.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self (name and role), confirms identity against the wristband and gains consent.
Calm, empathic approach to a frightened patient: acknowledges his fear of a heart attack, uses plain language and explains what they are doing.
History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Site and onset: central and right-sided, sudden, about 30 minutes ago.
Character, severity and radiation: sharp, 5/10, no radiation.
Pleuritic (worse on deep breathing), not eased by paracetamol or changing position.

check.x: Asks about breathlessness and finds it began about 2 hours ago, before the pain.
Asks about the legs and finds a painful, swollen, red right calf since last night.
Asks about other features of PE: cough, coughing up blood, fainting or near-fainting, palpitations.
Screens for differentials from at least four systems:

kids.x: Cardiovascular: screens for ACS (crushing pain, radiation to arm/neck/jaw, sweating, nausea) and aortic dissection (tearing pain to the back).
Cardiovascular: relief sitting forward (pericarditis); orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling (heart failure).
Respiratory: fever and productive cough (pneumonia); sudden breathlessness or pleuritic pain suggesting pneumothorax.
Gastrointestinal: burning retrosternal pain, reflux, link to food, trouble swallowing, epigastric pain and vomiting.
Musculoskeletal and psychological: chest injury in the fall, a localised tender spot; anxiety or panic symptoms.

check.x: Establishes reduced mobilisation since surgery (mostly in bed, up only to the toilet).
Explores the admission: mechanism (fall from about 2 metres off scaffolding at work), other injuries, the operation and any complications.
Asks about other VTE risk factors: previous DVT or PE, cancer, family history of clots, weight.
Takes a medication and allergy history relevant to anticoagulation:

kids.x: Identifies the thromboprophylaxis (enoxaparin injections) and asks whether any doses were missed.
Analgesia: regular paracetamol and ibuprofen when needed.
Allergies, including to iodinated contrast (none).
Bleeding risk: wound ooze, black stools, blood in urine, previous bleeding problems.

check.x: Past history (appendicectomy at 14) and family history (parental hypertension, father's bowel cancer this year, no clots in the family).
Social history: quantifies smoking (20 a day since age 20, about 27 pack-years), alcohol, occupation and who is at home.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: no idea of the cause, worried it is a heart attack.
Examination
Asks for the observations early, including oxygen saturation, and compares them with the normal morning set.
General inspection: distress, work of breathing, ability to speak in sentences, cyanosis, sweating, body habitus.
Cardiovascular: pulse rate and rhythm, blood pressure in both arms, JVP, heart sounds (loud P2, murmur, rub), right ventricular heave, peripheral perfusion.
Respiratory: trachea, expansion, percussion and auscultation (reduced air entry, crackles, pleural rub); palpates the chest wall for tenderness.
Examines and compares both legs: calf swelling (circumference 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity), pitting oedema, warmth, redness, tenderness along the deep veins.
Inspects the right hip wound for bleeding, haematoma or infection.
Investigations

Calculates the Wells score (signs of DVT 3, PE most likely 3, heart rate over 100 1.5, surgery within 4 weeks 1.5 = 9, high probability) and states D-dimer is not indicated: a high pre-test probability goes straight to imaging, and D-dimer is raised after surgery anyway.
Requests the right investigations:

kids.x: 12-lead ECG.
FBE, UEC, LFT and coagulation studies, with a high-sensitivity troponin and a repeat troponin at 2 to 3 hours.
Requests CT pulmonary angiogram as the definitive test.
Venous duplex ultrasound of the right leg if CTPA is delayed or contraindicated (a proximal DVT would justify treatment); not needed to guide treatment once CTPA confirms PE.

check.x: Names V/Q scan as the alternative if there is contrast allergy, severe renal impairment or pregnancy.
Interpretation

Gives PE from a right leg DVT as the diagnosis and justifies it: day 5 after surgery, immobility, obesity, smoking, sudden pleuritic pain, breathlessness, unilateral calf swelling, tachycardia and low saturation.

Observations: heart rate 124, respiratory rate 26 and SpO2 93% on air are in the yellow zone (Clinical Review), new since the morning; blood pressure and conscious state are normal, so he is not shocked; escalates to a senior, and a rapid response is called for any red-zone value.

ECG and bloods: ECG shows sinus tachycardia, no ischaemic changes or right heart strain, unchanged from the pre-operative ECG apart from the rate; states there is no STEMI, that ACS is made less likely together with the troponin (repeat due), and that a near-normal ECG does not exclude PE. Bloods: normal renal function (safe for contrast, no dose adjustment), normal platelets (safe to anticoagulate, HIT unlikely on enoxaparin), normal coagulation, expected post-operative haemoglobin, initial troponin normal (repeat at 2-3 h).

CTPA: confirms bilateral lower lobe pulmonary emboli with a small right lower lobe infarct and effusion, no CT signs of right ventricular strain, and no other cause (no pneumothorax, pneumonia or rib fracture).

Classifies it as a haemodynamically stable, intermediate-low risk PE (sPESI 1 from HR ≥110; no RV dysfunction, troponin normal): admit and monitor, anticoagulate, no thrombolysis; and as provoked by surgery and immobility.
Management
Immediate care: ABCDE, continuous monitoring, oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92% (target 92 to 96%), IV access, analgesia (paracetamol, with a cautious opioid if needed).
Escalates promptly to the orthopaedic registrar or consultant and discusses surgical bleeding risk before therapeutic anticoagulation.
Anticoagulation:

kids.x: Starts therapeutic anticoagulation promptly (ideally before imaging given the high probability), after agreeing bleeding risk with the orthopaedic team.

Stops prophylactic enoxaparin and names one therapeutic regimen: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcut 12-hourly, apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily, or rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily.
States 3 months of treatment for PE provoked by major surgery.

check.x: Stops ibuprofen because of the bleeding risk with anticoagulation and reviews analgesia.

States that if he becomes unstable (systolic below 90, shock), they would call a rapid response and involve ICU and seniors to consider reperfusion, noting recent major surgery raises the bleeding risk of thrombolysis.

Explains in plain words: not a heart attack, a clot from the leg has travelled to the lungs, the blood thinner injections lower but do not remove the risk, and the treatment plan, including getting moving with the physio once anticoagulated.
Optional extra: offers smoking cessation support (nicotine replacement in hospital, Quitline 13 78 48) and explains smoking raises clot risk.
Safety netting
Tells Chong and the nurse what to report straight away in hospital, in plain words:

kids.x: Worsening PE: worse breathlessness or chest pain, feeling faint, coughing blood; asks for regular observations and a rapid response call for any red-zone value.
Bleeding on anticoagulation: bleeding from the wound, black or bloody stools, blood in urine or vomit, a severe headache or any head knock.

check.x: Discharge and follow-up: after discharge, call 000 for sudden breathlessness, chest pain or collapse and go to ED for significant bleeding; GP letter and review within 1 to 2 weeks; review at 3 months about stopping. Extras (credit if given): take every dose, avoid NSAIDs, discuss return to building work and heights while anticoagulated.

part2.lead: Here are the results of the investigations: Chong's observations, his ECG, his blood results, and the CT pulmonary angiogram report from an hour later.
part2.patient:
Chong is still in the room. If the candidate has not covered them, ask one at a time:

  • "So it's not a heart attack?"
  • "I've been having the blood thinner injections every night. How did I still get a clot?"
  • Only if time remains: "How long will I be on these blood thinners, and when can I get back on the tools?"

You are relieved if told clearly it is not a heart attack, and settle if the plan is explained in plain words.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: On room air throughout. 08:00 set: HR 84, BP 130/82, RR 16, SpO2 97%, T 36.8 °C (all white zone).
handover.model:
Read: at 14:20 heart rate 124 (yellow), respiratory rate 26 (yellow) and SpO2 93% on room air (yellow); blood pressure 132/84, temperature 37.6 °C and conscious state normal (white). The 14:50 set is unchanged. The morning set was normal, so this is new.

For Chong: each yellow-zone value calls for a Clinical Review, which is this review, with escalation to the registrar. Tachycardia, tachypnoea and low saturation fit PE. A normal, maintained blood pressure means he is haemodynamically stable (not high-risk PE). SpO2 93% is within the 92 to 96% target, so oxygen is not essential yet.

What it changes: continuous monitoring and frequent observations. Any red-zone value, such as a falling blood pressure, worsening saturation or confusion, calls for a rapid response.

rows.note: New chest pain reported; resident called

handover.label: 12-lead ECG (14:30)
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, resting, 14:30.

  • Rate 122 beats/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus tachycardia.
  • Axis: +70°.
  • PR interval 148 ms.
  • QRS 90 ms; no bundle branch block.
  • QTc 438 ms.
  • ST segments: no elevation or depression in any territory.
  • T waves: inverted in V1 only (present on the previous ECG); upright elsewhere.
  • Other: no S1Q3T3 pattern, no right axis deviation, no right ventricular strain pattern, no pathological Q waves.
  • Comparison: pre-operative ECG 5 days ago showed sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min, otherwise identical. The only change is the rate.
handover.model:
Read: sinus tachycardia at 122, normal axis and intervals, no ST changes, isolated T inversion in V1 that was there before (a normal variant), no right heart strain pattern. Unchanged apart from the rate.

For Chong: no ST elevation in any territory, so no STEMI. With no new ischaemic changes and the initial normal troponin (repeat due at 2 to 3 hours), ACS is made less likely, which answers his fear of a heart attack. Sinus tachycardia is the commonest ECG finding in PE; a near-normal ECG does not exclude PE, and the absence of right heart strain fits a stable PE.

What it changes: no STEMI pathway or urgent cardiology referral; proceed with the PE pathway and repeat the troponin.

handover.label: Blood results (collected 14:35)
handover.result: Collected 14:35, about 45 minutes after the onset of pain.
handover.model:
Read: haemoglobin 121 g/L, low but stable since day 1 after surgery (expected blood loss); white cells and platelets normal (platelets 298, above the pre-operative 260); INR and APTT normal; fibrinogen and CRP mildly raised, as expected after surgery; sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine (eGFR above 90) and liver tests normal; high-sensitivity troponin T 8 ng/L, below the 99th centile.

For Chong: normal renal function means contrast for the CTPA is safe and enoxaparin or a DOAC needs no dose adjustment. A normal, rising platelet count on day 5 of enoxaparin makes heparin-induced thrombocytopenia unlikely and allows anticoagulation. Normal coagulation and a stable haemoglobin mean no bleeding problem. The troponin was taken only about 45 minutes after onset, so a single value below the 99th centile does not on its own rule out ACS or right ventricular injury.

What it changes: no barrier to CTPA or therapeutic anticoagulation; repeat the hs-troponin at 2 to 3 hours; these are the baseline values for monitoring haemoglobin and platelets on treatment.

handover.label: CT pulmonary angiogram report
handover.result:
Examination: CT pulmonary angiogram, with intravenous iodinated contrast (70 mL) timed to the pulmonary arteries. eGFR above 90.

Clinical details: 47-year-old man, day 5 after fixation of a right neck of femur fracture. Sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, heart rate 124, SpO2 93% on room air, swollen right calf. Wells score 9.

Comparison: none.

Findings:

  • Pulmonary arteries: main pulmonary artery 26 mm (normal). Filling defect in the right lower lobe pulmonary artery extending into the right lower lobe segmental arteries, occlusive in the posterior basal segmental artery. Non-occlusive filling defect in the left lower lobe lateral basal segmental artery. No thrombus in the main or right and left pulmonary arteries.
  • Right heart: right to left ventricular diameter ratio 0.8. No flattening or bowing of the interventricular septum. No reflux of contrast into the inferior vena cava or hepatic veins.
  • Lungs: 25 mm wedge-shaped, pleural-based opacity in the right posterior basal segment, in keeping with early pulmonary infarction. No other consolidation. No pneumothorax.
  • Pleura: small right pleural effusion.
  • Mediastinum and aorta: no lymphadenopathy. Thoracic aorta of normal calibre (study timed for the pulmonary arteries, not a dedicated aortic study).
  • Bones and upper abdomen: no rib fracture. Upper abdomen unremarkable.

Conclusion: acute bilateral lower lobe pulmonary emboli (right lobar and segmental, left segmental) with a small right lower lobe pulmonary infarct and small right effusion. No CT evidence of right ventricular strain. Result phoned to the requesting resident.
handover.model:
Read: clots in the right lower lobe artery and its segmental branches and a left lower lobe segmental branch, with no saddle or main pulmonary artery thrombus. The right to left ventricular ratio is below 1 with no septal flattening or contrast reflux, so no right ventricular strain. The wedge-shaped opacity and small effusion are a pulmonary infarct, which explains the right-sided pleuritic pain and the dullness at the right base. No pneumothorax, pneumonia or rib fracture.

For Chong: PE is confirmed, almost certainly from the right calf DVT and provoked by surgery and immobility. With normal blood pressure he is haemodynamically stable, and this is an intermediate-low risk PE (sPESI 1 from HR ≥110; no RV dysfunction, troponin normal): admit and monitor, anticoagulate, no thrombolysis.

What it changes: therapeutic anticoagulation agreed with the orthopaedic team, 3 months for a provoked PE, and monitoring on the ward. The leg ultrasound will not change treatment now the CTPA is positive.

ask: What is your diagnosis, how do you justify it, and how severe is the PE?
What is your management, including anticoagulation (and when would you have started anticoagulation relative to the CTPA?), who you would involve, and what you would do if he became unstable?
How would you answer Chong's questions, and what safety netting and follow-up would you arrange?

guide:
Start Part 1 by giving the nurse's report. Give the 14:20 observations only when the candidate asks for them. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Chong stays stable in Part 1, whatever the candidate does. Investigations belong to Part 1: if the candidate reaches the last minute without saying which investigations they would request, prompt once: "Which investigations would you request, and why?" Mark the Wells score, D-dimer decision and investigation items (25 to 27) there. Credit a candidate who says in Part 1 that they would start anticoagulation before the CTPA; mark item 37.1 wherever it comes up.

Part 2 is tight. Hand over all four results together and ask the questions in order. Let Chong ask his first two questions if the candidate has not answered them, and the third only if time remains. Item 41 (smoking) and the extras in item 44 are not essential; do not hold the candidate back to earn them.

Item 9 needs differentials from at least four systems. The ACS and dissection screen (9.1) is the critical part; the pericarditis and heart-failure questions (9.2) earn credit but are not critical.

A high-performing candidate finds the 2 hours of breathlessness and the swollen right calf, links them to day 5 after surgery, immobility, obesity and smoking, asks about the enoxaparin, and examines both legs. They give a Wells score of 9 and request a CTPA without a D-dimer. In Part 2 they read the observations by chart zone, note the early troponin needs repeating, and confirm a stable, intermediate-low risk PE with no right heart strain. They escalate to the orthopaedic team about bleeding risk, start therapeutic anticoagulation, stop the ibuprofen, plan 3 months of treatment, and give clear red flags for clotting and for bleeding.

A borderline candidate takes a cardiac-only history, misses the leg, orders a D-dimer and waits for it, treats the ECG or a single early troponin as excluding PE or ACS, keeps the prophylactic enoxaparin running as treatment, or starts anticoagulation without considering the surgical bleeding risk.
explain:
Diagnosis: pulmonary embolism from a right leg DVT

Chong is day 5 after major orthopaedic surgery for a hip fracture and has hardly mobilised. He is obese (BMI 31) and smokes 20 a day. He has had breathlessness for 2 hours, then sudden sharp, central and right-sided, pleuritic chest pain, and a painful, swollen, red right calf since last night. On examination he has tachycardia, tachypnoea, low saturation and a right calf 4 cm larger than the left. This is PE from a right leg DVT until proven otherwise. Surgery, trauma and immobilisation are provoking risk factors. PE can occur despite pharmacological thromboprophylaxis, which reduces the risk but does not remove it.

Differentials that matter

  • Cardiovascular: ACS (crushing pain, radiation, sweating, nausea), aortic dissection (tearing pain to the back, unequal arm pressures), pericarditis (pleuritic, eased by sitting forward), arrhythmia, heart failure.
  • Respiratory: pneumothorax (trauma, sudden pleuritic pain), pneumonia (fever, productive cough; post-operative patients are at risk).
  • Gastrointestinal: reflux, oesophageal spasm, pancreatitis.
  • Musculoskeletal and psychological: rib fracture or chest wall strain (reproducible tenderness), panic attack.

Pre-test probability and investigations

The Wells criteria score clinical signs of DVT (3), PE as the most likely diagnosis (3), heart rate over 100 (1.5), immobilisation or surgery in the last 4 weeks (1.5), previous DVT or PE (1.5), haemoptysis (1) and malignancy (1). Chong scores 9, high probability. With low to moderate probability, a negative D-dimer can exclude PE and a positive one leads to CTPA. With high probability, D-dimer is not needed and the next step is CTPA. D-dimer helps rule out, not rule in, and it is raised after surgery anyway. V/Q scanning is the alternative when there is contrast allergy, severe renal impairment or pregnancy. A venous duplex ultrasound confirms the DVT; a proximal DVT in a patient with suspected PE supports treatment when CTPA cannot be done. The ECG is mainly to look for ACS and may show sinus tachycardia or right heart strain. FBE, UEC, LFT and coagulation studies are the baseline before anticoagulation and look for infection or electrolyte problems. A high-sensitivity troponin taken soon after the onset of pain needs repeating at 2 to 3 hours; a single early value below the 99th centile does not rule out ACS or myocardial injury.

Interpreting his results

Three observations are in the yellow zone of the NSW Between the Flags chart (heart rate 124, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 93%), which calls for a Clinical Review with escalation. His blood pressure is normal, so he is not shocked. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia only. Renal function, platelets and coagulation are normal, so contrast and anticoagulation are safe; normal platelets on day 5 of enoxaparin make heparin-induced thrombocytopenia unlikely. The initial troponin is normal but was taken about 45 minutes after onset, so it is repeated. The CTPA confirms bilateral lower lobe emboli with a small infarct (the right-sided pleuritic pain) and no right ventricular strain. A heart rate of 110 or more gives a simplified PESI of 1, so he does not meet the low-risk criteria; with no right ventricular dysfunction and a normal troponin, this is an intermediate-low risk PE. He should be admitted and monitored on the ward and anticoagulated, rather than go home early, and thrombolysis is not indicated.

Management

  • Immediate: ABCDE, monitoring, IV access, oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92% (target 92 to 96%), and analgesia. Stop the ibuprofen.
  • Involve seniors: the orthopaedic registrar or consultant decides on surgical bleeding risk before therapeutic anticoagulation. Document and hand over.
  • Haemodynamically stable PE (eTG): anticoagulate. With high clinical probability, start without waiting for imaging unless contraindicated. Stop prophylactic enoxaparin and use a therapeutic regimen: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcut 12-hourly, apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily, or rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily. Choose the agent with the surgical team; LMWH is often used first in the early post-operative period.
  • Duration: 3 months for VTE provoked by a major transient risk factor such as surgery.
  • Unstable PE (sustained hypotension or shock): rapid response, ICU and senior input, and reperfusion with systemic thrombolysis or interventional procedures. Recent major surgery raises the bleeding risk of thrombolysis and weighs in that decision.
  • Other: mobilise with the physiotherapist once anticoagulated, give nicotine replacement and quit support, and explain honestly why a clot happened despite prophylaxis.

Safety netting and follow-up

In hospital, Chong and the nurse should report worsening breathlessness or chest pain, faintness or coughing blood straight away, and any red-zone observation calls for a rapid response. On anticoagulation he should report wound bleeding, black or bloody stools, blood in the urine or vomit, or any head injury or severe headache. After discharge, he calls 000 for sudden breathlessness, chest pain or collapse, and goes to ED for significant bleeding. He should take every dose and avoid NSAIDs. Send a discharge letter to his GP for review within 1 to 2 weeks and a review at 3 months about stopping. Discuss fall and injury risk on building sites while he is anticoagulated.
points: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after surgery, with a swollen calf, is PE until proven otherwise; thromboprophylaxis lowers the risk but does not remove it.
Use the Wells score: when PE is likely, go straight to CTPA. D-dimer only rules out PE at lower probability, and it is raised after surgery.
Blood pressure decides the treatment: stable PE needs anticoagulation; hypotension or shock needs a rapid response and consideration of reperfusion.
After surgery, agree the bleeding risk with the surgical team, stop prophylactic enoxaparin and NSAIDs, and start a therapeutic dose. A PE provoked by surgery is treated for 3 months.
A near-normal ECG and a normal troponin do not exclude PE. The ECG is mainly to look for ACS and right heart strain.
Before anticoagulating, check renal function (contrast and dosing), platelets (HIT on heparin) and coagulation.
